evidence.excerpt: Machine breakdowns introduce capacity uncertainty that static lead-time quotation and pricing models ignore. This paper reports a discrete-event simulation study of a six-machine job shop with three job classes, modelled in Arena. Four pricing policies are compared: fixed price with first-come first-served sequencing; fixed price with shortest-processing-time priority; workload-triggered price steps; and a continuous price function of current queue length. Machine unavailability is modelled with Weibull-distributed time-to-failure drawn from maintenance records of a Vojvodina engineering company. Over 200 replications of a 90-day horizon, the continuous pricing policy achieves a 14.3% higher net revenue than fixed pricing while holding average customer waiting time approximately constant. The workload-step policy performs similarly but requires only three price tiers, suggesting practical implementability. Results are sensitive to the assumed demand elasticity; the paper conducts a parametric sweep over the range estimated in earlier stated-preference work.
